**On Margins**

If you are asked to write about anything at all, the first thing you notice is how much the blank page pushes back. Freedom is a strange kind of pressure. The page has no subject, no shape, no edges except the ones you impose on it, and so before long you find yourself looking for a wall to lean against. I would like to lean against the margin.

I mean the literal one: the strip of empty paper that runs around the printed text on every page of every book you own. You have looked at tens of thousands of them and probably never looked at one. That is what a margin is for. It is the part of the page whose whole job is not to be read. And yet it has a history, and a design, and a secret life as the place where readers have always done their most honest writing.

Start with the fact that it is there at all. Paper costs money; parchment cost a great deal more. A medieval scribe working on a Bible might have been using the skins of several hundred animals, each one scraped, stretched, and cut. Every square inch was expensive. And yet those pages have margins so generous they look almost wasteful—the text block sitting like a small island in a sea of blank vellum. Part of this was practical. The edges of parchment are the weakest part; they fray, they get thumbed, they are what the binder trims. A wide margin is a buffer zone between the words and the world. But part of it was aesthetic, and the aesthetics were surprisingly precise. There was a canon, passed from workshop to workshop, that fixed the proportions of the text block to the page: the inner margin narrowest, the top a little wider, the outer wider still, and the bottom widest of all. The page, in other words, was built to feel heavier at the bottom and to open outward, so that when the book lay flat the two facing text blocks seemed to lean gently toward each other across the gutter. Jan Tschichold, the twentieth-century typographer who spent years reverse-engineering these proportions from surviving manuscripts, argued that they were not arbitrary at all but geometric—derived with a compass and a straightedge from the diagonals of the page itself. He called the result "the secret canon," and he was a little indignant that nobody had bothered to write it down. It had simply been known, the way carpenters know things.

So the margin is designed. It is not what was left over after the words ran out; it is what the words were fitted into. This is worth remembering, because everything else about margins tends to make them look accidental.

Consider the school exercise book, the one with a red vertical line ruled a couple of centimeters from the left edge. Almost every literate person alive learned to write inside that line. The line was not for you. It was for the teacher, who would put ticks and corrections and small disappointed comments in the space you had been told to leave empty. Which means that the first margin most of us encountered was a place where someone else had the right to write and we did not. You wrote the text; authority wrote the margin. It is a curious arrangement, and I suspect it has something to do with why writing in the margins of a book feels, even to adults who own the book outright, faintly transgressive. It feels like sitting in the teacher's chair.

The word "marginalia" itself is younger than you would guess. Samuel Taylor Coleridge is usually credited with popularizing it, in the 1810s, and the fact that it needed popularizing tells you something. People had been scribbling in books for a thousand years, but they had not thought of the scribbles as a *thing*—a genre, a category with a Latin plural. Coleridge did, largely because his own were so extraordinary that his friends started lending him books in the hope he would annotate them. He would write on the flyleaves, down the sides, upside down along the bottom, in pencil and in ink, arguing with the author, agreeing with the author, digressing into theology, remembering something Wordsworth had said. When his marginalia were finally collected they ran to six fat volumes. A man had produced a substantial body of work entirely on the edges of other people's.

But the medieval margins are the ones that stay with me, because they are so alive. There are the glosses, of course—the layers of commentary that grew around legal and scriptural texts until the original sat in the center like a small pond surrounded by dense reeds of interpretation, each generation of scholars writing in smaller script around the writing of the last. That is one kind of marginal life, and it is serious. But there is another kind, which is not serious at all. Open a fourteenth-century psalter and in the lower margin, beneath a solemn Latin prayer, you may find a rabbit riding a snail, or a knight fleeing in terror from a snail, or a monkey playing bagpipes, or a naked man with a trumpet where no trumpet should be. Art historians have spent careers on these "drolleries" without agreeing on what they mean. Some argue they are moral inversions, the world turned upside down to remind the reader of proper order. Some think they are jokes, and that the illuminators, who were paid by the page and worked long hours in bad light, were simply amusing themselves. The snail thing in particular—armed knights cowering before a common garden snail, over and over, across a whole century of manuscripts—has never been satisfactorily explained. It may have been a running gag whose punchline is lost. There is something wonderful in that: a joke that was funny for a hundred years, preserved perfectly in gold leaf, whose meaning has evaporated completely, leaving only the fact that someone, once, was laughing.

And then there are the scribes' own notes, which are not jokes but complaints. Medieval copyists sometimes left remarks in the margins or at the ends of their texts, and they are almost unbearably human. "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink." "The parchment is hairy." "Oh, my hand." "Thank God it will soon be dark." "I am very cold." One Irish scribe, working through some tedious Latin grammar, wrote in the margin in his own language a small poem about his white cat, Pangur, who hunted mice while he hunted words, each of them content in his own craft. The poem is better than the grammar. It has outlasted it. Nobody reads the text that scribe was copying, but a thousand years later people are still reading about his cat.

This is the thing about margins that I find hardest to stop thinking about. The center of the page is where the official business happens, the thing that was commissioned, the thing that was meant to last. The margin is where the person shows up. And often it is the person we end up wanting.

Herman Melville's copy of Shakespeare survives, and it is dense with pencil marks. In the margins of *King Lear* he underlined and annotated with a kind of ferocity, and scholars have traced lines from those annotations straight into *Moby-Dick*, which he was writing at the time. You can watch, in a way, the book being born in the edges of another book. William Blake annotated his copy of the *Discourses* of Sir Joshua Reynolds, the reigning authority on painting in his day, and the annotations are a sustained act of fury: "This Man was Hired to Depress Art." Blake could have written an essay against Reynolds; he chose instead to write *on* Reynolds, so that his contempt would sit forever pressed against the sentences that provoked it. Mark Twain, in a book of essays that irritated him, wrote in the margin: "Idiot." That is the whole note. There is no context you could add that would improve it.

The most famous marginal note in history is, fittingly, about the margin's own limits. Pierre de Fermat, reading his copy of Diophantus's *Arithmetica* sometime around 1637, came to a problem about splitting a square into two squares and wrote beside it that he had found a truly marvelous proof that the same could not be done for any higher power—cubes, fourth powers, and so on—but that *hanc marginis exiguitas non caperet*: the narrowness of this margin would not contain it. He then died without writing the proof anywhere else. Mathematicians spent three hundred and fifty-eight years trying to reconstruct it. When Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in 1995, his proof ran to well over a hundred pages and used mathematics that did not exist in Fermat's lifetime, which has led most people to conclude that Fermat did not actually have a valid proof at all, or had one for a special case and got carried away. He was, in other words, doing exactly what people do in margins: overstating, gesturing, leaving a note to himself that he never expected anyone to read. The difference is that the whole history of number theory ended up hanging on the size of a strip of paper in a book he owned.

I love that the margin was too small. I love that this is the excuse. Nobody has ever written "this text block is too narrow to contain my proof." The center of the page is assumed to be sufficient; it is the edge that runs out. And yet the edge is where the interesting claim got made.

There is a whole vocabulary that grows out of this geography, and it is worth noticing how loaded it is. To be *marginal* is to be unimportant. To *marginalize* someone is to push them to the edge where they will not be read. A *marginal* seat is one that could go either way, a *marginal* gain is one barely worth having, a *marginal* note is one you can skip. The whole set of metaphors assumes that value lives in the center and drains away toward the border. This is a very natural assumption for a species that prints text in the middle of the page. But it does not survive much contact with actual pages. The center is where the prayer is; the margin is where the man with the trumpet is. The center is Reynolds; the margin is Blake. The center is the Latin grammar; the margin is the cat.

I do not want to overstate this. Most marginalia is dull—"good point," "cf. p. 42," a wavy line meaning roughly *hmm*. Anyone who has bought a used textbook knows the specific despair of inheriting a stranger's highlighting, the pale yellow bars marching across every sentence as though the previous owner had decided the whole book was important and therefore none of it was. The margin is not automatically a place of genius. It is only a place of freedom, and freedom produces mostly ordinary things, with the occasional Pangur.

The digital page has, oddly, both abolished margins and turned everything into one. Text on a screen reflows to fit whatever window you give it; there is no fixed edge, no canon of proportions, nothing designed to hold the thumb. You cannot write on it in the old sense. And yet the apparatus of marginal commentary has metastasized. Kindle will show you, with a faint dotted underline, the sentences that other readers have highlighted most—a kind of crowd-sourced marginalia, anonymous and aggregate, telling you that fourteen thousand people paused here. Every article online drags behind it a comments section that is, structurally, a margin: the space beneath and beside the official text where the readers get to talk back. Most of it is the equivalent of "Idiot," without Twain's economy. But the impulse is identical, and it is very old. People have never been able to read without wanting to answer.

What interests me is that the answering happens at the edge, not in the middle. You do not, as a rule, cross out the author's sentence and write your own in its place. You leave the text intact and write *beside* it. The margin is a form of respect and a form of dissent at once. It says: I will not touch what you made, but I will not let it stand alone either. There is something in this that feels like the right relationship between a reader and a text, and maybe between a person and the world—not to overwrite, not to defer, but to annotate.

The typographers understood something the metaphors miss. Tschichold's secret canon does not treat the margin as waste. It treats the margin as the thing that makes the text readable at all. A page with no margins is unbearable; the eye has nowhere to rest, the words crowd to the edge and seem to be falling off. The blank space is not the absence of design. It *is* the design. It is the reason the text looks like it belongs where it is. And the classical proportions, with their heavy bottom and open outer edge, are not about the text at all; they are about the hand that holds the book and the eye that travels down the page and needs, at the end, a little room to land.

So perhaps the margin is best understood not as the edge of the page but as the part of the page that acknowledges there is a reader. The text block addresses itself to everyone, or to no one, or to God. The margin addresses itself to whoever is actually holding the thing, and it does so by leaving them room. It is an invitation with nothing written on it. That is why the snail is there, and the cat, and Fermat's overconfident note, and the tired scribe's plea for a drink. They are all replies to the same invitation. The book left a space, and someone stepped into it.

I was asked to write freely, and I have spent my freedom on the strip of white around other people's words, which is probably a confession of some kind. But it does not feel like a small subject. It feels like the place where writing has always been most free—not the commissioned center but the unruled edge, where nobody was watching and the parchment was hairy and the hand ached and, even so, someone thought it worth recording that the cat was good at his job. If the center is where we say what we are supposed to say, the margin is where we say what we noticed. I would rather be read there.
